title: Landscape scope, design boundaries and approvals
audience: Landscapers, designers and crew leaders who scope, quote and manage landscape projects from initial site visit to approval and handover.
learningOutcomes: Define the scope of a landscape job, separating design, supply, installation and maintenance.
Identify the approvals, permits and consents that a landscape project may need before work starts.
Recognise design elements that fall outside the business's scope, such as structures, retaining walls over the threshold, drainage connections and elements that need an engineer.
Record the scope, approvals and exclusions in a form the client signs and the crew can follow.

instruction.heading: What a landscape scope covers
instruction.body: Landscaping covers a wide range of work, from a simple garden refresh to a full backyard transformation with paving, planting, lighting, drainage and structures. The scope is the first and most important document, because it decides what is designed, what is supplied, what is installed and what is maintained afterwards. Separate these four parts in the quote. Design means preparing a layout, plant list and materials list. Supply means providing plants, stone, soil or hard materials. Installation means the physical work on site. Maintenance means the care after installation, usually for a set period. A client who understands the four parts is less likely to expect the business to do work it has not quoted, and the crew knows exactly what it is building. Confirm the scope in writing before any materials are ordered.

instruction.heading: Site information and design boundaries
instruction.body: Before designing, gather the site information. Measure the site and draw a plan with the boundary, the levels, the existing trees and plants, the existing structures, the services, the drainage paths, the access route and the orientation. Note the soil type and any visible drainage problems. Identify the features the client wants to keep. Design boundaries are the limits that the business will not cross without another party's input. A plant layout is generally within a landscape design. A new structure, a retaining wall above the threshold, an outdoor kitchen with gas, an electrical lighting circuit or a stormwater connection is not.

instruction.heading: Approvals, permits and consents
instruction.body: Many landscape projects need an approval before work begins, and a crew that starts without checking can face stop orders, forced removal of work and disputes with the client. Common approval points include building permits for new structures above the thresholds set by the local authority, consents for work that affects trees or native vegetation, approvals for works near public land, and strata or body corporate approval for common property. Two state positions were checked. In New South Wales, residential structural landscaping work valued over $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST, needs a contractor licence. The listed work includes retaining walls outside habitable buildings, whatever their material, and decks, pergolas and other non-habitable structures (page updated 23 June 2026). In Victoria, a retaining wall under 1 metre generally needs no building permit, unless it forms part of other building works or protects neighbouring land (practice note dated April 2022). Make the approval check part of the design stage, not a last-minute step. Record the authority, the application reference, the status and the person responsible for chasing it. Do not allow construction to start on an element until its approval is in writing.

instruction.heading: Writing the scope and handling change
instruction.body: Write a scope document that lists the design items, the supply items, the installation items and the maintenance items, each with quantities and a clear description. List the exclusions, including the items that need approval or licensed work. Include the access arrangements, the working hours, the waste removal, the site protection and the payment milestones. Attach the plan and the plant or material list, and ask the client to sign or confirm them. Changes during the project are variations. A variation must be written, priced and approved before the extra work is done. Keep the variation with the original scope so that the handover can compare what was agreed with what was built.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the scope document against the site plan and the approvals list. A competent designer or crew leader can explain each part of the scope, identify the approvals that may be needed, name the exclusions and describe the variation process. Escalate any design element that appears to need an engineer, a building permit or a licence holder, any request to change a structure after approval, and any site where the services or the boundary are not clear.

procedure: Visit the site and record the boundary, levels, existing plants and structures, services, drainage and access.
Confirm the client's goals, the features to keep and the budget range, without promising a price before the design is scoped.
Prepare a plan that separates design, supply, installation and maintenance items, and mark the excluded elements.
Identify the approvals, permits and consents that the project may need, and record the authority that issues each one.
Confirm the services locations and access before any digging or material placement.
Write the scope document with quantities, exclusions, access, waste, site protection and payment milestones.
Obtain the client's written confirmation of the scope and the plan before ordering materials.
Record every variation in writing, priced and approved before the extra work begins.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a new garden plan that includes a timber pergola, a retaining wall to level a sloping area, and a gas outdoor heater.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you scope the plan, and which items are excluded or referred?
workedExamples.reasoning: The planting, paving and soft landscape can be scoped within the business's design and installation work. The pergola may need a building permit or approval, depending on size and location, and that must be confirmed with the council. The retaining wall needs a height and loading check and may need an engineer, so it is referred. The gas heater needs a gas licence holder and is excluded. Mark each excluded item on the plan, write the referral, and confirm the in-scope items with the client.

workedExamples.situation: Halfway through a project, the client asks for a small garden path to be moved to the other side of the lawn, which crosses a drainage line.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before moving the path?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the change until it is scoped and approved. Check the drainage line on the site plan, and confirm whether it is a stormwater or drainage connection that needs a licence holder or a check by the council. Record the request as a variation, quote it, and get written approval before any work starts. Do not move the path across the drainage line without that approval.

equipmentAndPpe: Site survey tools, such as measuring tape, level and survey stakes
Plan template and design software or drawing tools
Scope document template with exclusions and variations
Camera or phone for recording the site, with consent
High-visibility clothing and footwear for site visits

commonErrors.error: Quoting a structure or a retaining wall without checking whether an approval or engineer is needed.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the approvals and engineering needs before quoting, and mark items that need referral as excluded.

commonErrors.error: Starting work on a verbal scope and changing the scope as the project develops.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the scope in writing before ordering materials, and handle every change as a written variation.

commonErrors.error: Missing a service or drainage line on the site plan.
commonErrors.prevention: Locate services before design and before digging, and record them on the plan.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a design is approved because the client likes it.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the approvals required, record who issues them, and confirm the status before construction.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Structures, retaining walls, gas and electrical elements, and stormwater connections can need approval, engineering input or licensed work. Victoria: a retaining wall under 1 metre generally needs no building permit (April 2022). New South Wales: residential structural landscaping over $5,000 including GST needs a contractor licence (23 June 2026).
This lesson does not grant any building, design, engineering, plumbing, gas or electrical licence or approval.
Before any excavation, the service-locating procedure must be completed for the site. Buried services can be live or pressurised.

qualityStandard: The scope document separates design, supply, installation and maintenance, with quantities and exclusions.
Each approval that may apply is listed with the issuing authority and its status.
Every excluded or referred element is marked on the plan and in the scope.
The client has confirmed the scope and plan in writing before materials are ordered.
documentationEvidence: Site survey and plan with services, levels, drainage and access.
Signed scope document with exclusions, variations and payment milestones.
Approvals list with the status of each approval and the issuing authority.
Variation records with the client's written approval.
summary: Separate design, supply, installation and maintenance in the scope.
Check approvals and engineering needs before quoting structures, walls, gas, electrical and drainage work.
Mark excluded and referred items on the plan and in the scope, and confirm the scope in writing.
Handle every change as a written variation, approved before the extra work begins.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants a retaining wall and a gas outdoor heater included in a garden plan. What is the correct scoping step?
options: Include both in the price so the client has one contract and the whole job is covered at once on the plan
Check the approvals and engineering needs, and mark the wall and the gas heater as referred or excluded in the scope.
Leave them off the plan and add them later without a note, since the client can ask for them later

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks to move a garden path across a drainage line after work has started. What should happen?
options: Move the path immediately, since it is a small change and the crew is already on the site today
Ask the neighbour whether the drainage line can be moved, since the neighbour knows where the pipes are
Stop the change, check the drainage line, record it as a variation and get written approval before any work.
